item.title: First Mathematical Runtime Analyses of Evolutionary Multitask Multi-Objective Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.21311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To facilitate the solving of complex problems, evolutionary multitask optimization is regarded as a promising technique due to its capacity for cross-task knowledge transfer. In contrast to empirical evidences, no mathematical runtime support exists for this technique within the domain of multi-objective optimization. In this work, we aim to fill this important gap. We analyze how the representative multiobjective multifactorial evolutionary algorithm (MO-MFEA) covers the Pareto fronts of two bi-objective problems simultaneously. For the two-task problem of maximizing the classic bi-objective OMM and the multimodal OJZJ benchmarks, the MO-MFEA requires only an expected runtime of $O(n^2 \log n)$---the same as optimizing the simple OMM alone---yet achieves a speedup by a factor of $\Theta(n^{k-1}/\log n)$ compared to optimizing OJZJ alone (with gap size $k$). Similarly, for the task pair comprising the classic LOTZ and the multimodal DLTB benchmarks, a speedup of $\Theta(n)$ is attained over optimizing DLTB alone, while the runtime matches that of optimizing LOTZ alone.
item.dc:creator: Danyang Zhang, Weijie Zheng

item.title: Beyond the Hamming Cliff: Compact Spatial Encodings Preserving Semantic Distance in Spiking Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.22083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By pre-processing input signals with Gray, Thermometer, Johnson and hybrid encodings before passing them to spiking neural networks running on SpiNNaker hardware, Davies et al.(2025) address the semantic-spatial disparity that causes the ``Hamming cliff'' in standard binary representations. Continuous semantic patterns are presented as a set of simultaneous spikes at the input layer, preserving ultra-low latency processing. Training the network on multiple continuous values under each scheme, and measuring accuracy, required homeostatic scaling and false-positive rates, shows that removing the cliff is necessary but not sufficient: Gray encoding removes it yet retains little global distance structure, whereas Thermometer and Johnson preserve semantic distance at a code width that grows with the value range. The proposed hybrid encodings contain all three as limiting cases of a single parameter, recovering most of that structure at a fraction of the width. The homeostatic factor is shown to set a radius of tolerance around each trained pattern, so that the choice of encoding alone decides which values the network treats as similar.
item.dc:creator: Sergio Davies, Muhammad Aitsam, Morgan-Tyler Stone, Alessandro Di Nuovo, Liangxiu Han

item.title: A restart rule for genetic algorithms based on Schnabel census
item.description: arXiv:2610.22211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A new adaptive restart rule for Genetic Algorithms (GAs) is considered. The rule is based on the Schnabel Census method, originally developed for statistical estimation of a size of animal population. In this paper, the Schnabel Census method is applied as a heuristic to estimate the number of different solutions that may be visited with positive probability, given the current distribution of offspring. The rule consists in restarting a GA as soon as the maximum likelihood estimate reaches the number of different solutions observed at the recent iterations. We demonstrate how the new restart rule can be applied in a GA with steady-state replacement scheme, using three different combinatorial optimization problems as examples. Computational experiments on well-known benchmarks show a statistically significant advantage of the GAs with the new restarting rule over the original versions of GAs. The new restart rule also tends to be superior to the well-known rule, which restarts an algorithm when the current iteration number is twice the number of iterations till the current best incumbent was found.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Eremeev A., Zakharova Yu. A restart rule for genetic algorithms based on Schnabel census. Siberian Electronic Mathematical Reports. 2026. Vol. 23, N 1. pp. 554-570
item.dc:creator: Anton Eremeev, Yulia Zakharova

item.title: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy with Weight Perturbation on MNIST
item.description: arXiv:2610.21665v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weight perturbation (WP) estimates learning directions from random parameter perturbations and a scalar change in loss, without backpropagating derivatives. We examine how batch size, training duration, and estimator stabilization affect its attainable accuracy in fully connected MNIST networks. In the shallow configuration, large-batch training reaches approximately 97\% test accuracy, compared with an early backpropagation (BP) reference near 97.5--98\%. The same comparison exposes a substantial efficiency gap: under a ten-epoch budget, shallow WP reaches 90.2\%, whereas the reported BP reference reaches 97.4\%. Epoch-indexed curves show diminishing returns from increasing batch size beyond 4,000. Learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbation-based updates also stabilize deeper networks, although their recorded results do not establish BP-level accuracy. We distinguish these empirical findings from a finite-horizon approximation argument: under stated regularity conditions, population WP can approximate a fixed gradient-descent trajectory arbitrarily closely at any fixed finite depth. Positive classification margins then suffice to preserve the reference predictions on a finite test set with arbitrarily high probability. Together, the results identify near-BP accuracy as a configuration- and budget-dependent possibility, rather than evidence of equal efficiency or an unconditional accuracy guarantee across depth.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Inoue

item.title: Attention over noisy examples: generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network
item.description: arXiv:2610.22191v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In Hebbian learning from examples a Hopfield network of $N$ neurons is not supplied with the $K$ archetypes it has to retrieve but with $M$ blurred examples of each, of quality $r$, and whether it can infer them depends on the load $\alpha=K/N$ (interference among them) and on the dataset entropy $\rho=(1-r^2)/(Mr^2)$ (how little the examples say about them). We transfer this protocol to the exponential Hopfield model, whose zero-temperature update is a step of softmax attention with the unlabelled examples as keys. A signal-to-noise analysis gives in closed form the overlap between the output and an unseen archetype, $m^{(1)}={\rm erf}(1/\sqrt{2\rho_{\rm eff}})$: the majority-rule law of the pairwise model at small load, with $\rho$ replaced by an attention entropy $\rho_{\rm eff}$ built from the weight the softmax gives to the correct class and the number of examples it spreads it over. Two consequences follow. First, in a window of inverse temperatures $\beta$ that widens as $\sqrt N$ the interference between archetypes is exponentially small in $N\beta$: the load drops out and the number of archetypes that can be learnt grows as $\exp(c\sqrt N)$. Second, learning fails differently: in the pairwise model through a spin-glass phase, in the exponential model through memorization: the softmax concentrates its weight on the training example closest to the input and returns it in place of the archetype. Seen from the input the softmax weights are those of the random energy model, and memorization is its freezing transition, at $\beta\sqrt{N(1-r^2)}\simeq\sqrt{2\ln M}$; it is measurable on a head whose keys are examples as the number of examples carrying weight. On MNIST the diagnostic follows the random-energy prediction; on fashion-MNIST it detects sub-clusters in the classes, and the best accuracy lies beyond the memorization threshold, where the softmax reads out a local sub-prototype.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Alemanno

item.title: T-GADE: Thermodynamical Generative-AI-Driven Evolution of LLM Artifacts
item.description: arXiv:2609.12286v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Introducing large language models (LLMs) into evolutionary computation enables semantic generation of candidates, but the classical problem of maintaining population diversity remains. Inspired by the thermodynamical genetic algorithm (TDGA), we propose T-GADE (Thermodynamical Generative-AI-Driven Evolution of LLM Artifacts), an evolutionary computation framework extended through LLMs. T-GADE keeps the notions of a population and genetic operators, takes structured artifacts generated by an LLM as individuals, and implements crossover and mutation as LLM operators. It further introduces the HoxLM, an LLM that attempts self-repair of an individual after evaluation and before survival selection; two update schemes, generational and steady-state; and Fermi-type and Bose-type occupancy rules that define solution identity and whether duplicates are permitted. Survival selection is unified as minimization of the free energy $F_T=\langle E\rangle-TH$, and the selection temperature $T$ explicitly controls the balance between quality and diversity. We tested an implementation example aligned with Evolution of Heuristics (EoH) on the online bin-packing task, where the excess is the bin count in excess of the volume lower bound, relative to that bound. The HoxLM-equipped configuration reached lower excess with fewer total LLM calls than EoH. In the preregistered comparison at 400 total calls it won 9 of 10 seed-paired runs, with a median sealed excess of 0.836% against 3.912%, and it was also better in the mean and in the worst case. Temperature controls the spread of the retained population under both update schemes, and a small positive temperature improves training quality over the collapsed $T=0$ point in the generational Bose-type scheme. The evolved heuristics are shown as readable scoring rules.
item.dc:creator: Kyoko Ogawa, Naoki Mori

item.title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Tasks, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2609.27650v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements, drawing on a search without a lower year limit and source-led updates through September 2026. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived tasks to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. The synthesis identifies complementary routes to progress: phonetic, acoustic and semantic targets preserve different aspects of a message; shared representations support reuse across recording conditions and tasks; and online communication increasingly depends on calibration, feedback and user control alongside decoding accuracy. Shared benchmarks enable algorithmic comparisons, while longitudinal studies reveal the demands of sustained use. We discuss these developments and their remaining limitations, then outline a prospective five-level trajectory from commands and language to meaning, scenarios and bidirectional cognitive exchange
item.dc:creator: Yiqian Yang, Yiqun Duan, Chenyu Liu, Yiqi Wang, Xinliang Zhou, Chin-Teng Lin, Yu Zhang

item.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14409v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.
item.dc:creator: Alex Gower
